headline: ACC Debt Bill Advances as MPs Clash Over Retrospective Claims and LNG Costs
summary: Parliament advanced legislation that would allow the Government to recover some past supplementary assistance from people receiving backdated ACC payments, prompting warnings about hardship for survivors and other claimants. MPs also clashed over the proposed LNG import facility and its possible effect on household power bills, while debating infrastructure priorities, food costs and new police powers for public places. The sitting was extended overnight, and the ACC bill is scheduled for its third reading next sitting day.

topicSummaries.topic: ACC Debt Bill Advances Despite Concerns About Survivors and Hardship
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill could affect about 37,500 people by enabling recovery of supplementary assistance from backdated ACC payments, with some claimants and their partners potentially facing debts.
topicSummaries.content: The Social Security (Accident Compensation and Calculation of Weekly Income) Amendment Bill would clarify how backdated ACC payments are counted against past welfare assistance and apply that approach retrospectively. Associate Social Development Minister Penny Simmonds said it aligns the law with longstanding policy and practice, and that MSD retains discretion over repayment arrangements, not whether a debt is established. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori argued that the change would entrench an unlawful practice identified by the courts and could deepen hardship, particularly for people with delayed sensitive claims. Labour cited an ACC sample of 50 cases in which 65 percent involved sensitive claims and 70 percent involved women; the Government said it did not hold claim reasons for all affected people. The Government amended the bill to preserve cases already in review or appeal, estimating the expansion would cover another 91 people at a cost of $2.1 million. The committee approved the bill with amendments by 68 votes to 54; its third reading is scheduled for the next sitting day.

keyExchanges.speaker: Helen White (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: What the Minister seeks to entrench here is the right of MSD to take back all those extra payments that MSD has made and not compensate that person with anything that ACC should have paid in the interim.

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Irrespective of what the source of income is, it needs to be treated fairly. New Zealanders need to know that the welfare system is based on income support for people when it is needed based on their income; all sources of income, not just some.

topicSummaries.topic: LNG Plan Faces Scrutiny as Middle East Conflict Raises Price Risks
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The cost and price exposure of a proposed LNG import facility could affect household electricity bills and the security of New Zealand’s energy supply.
topicSummaries.content: Opposition Leader Chris Hipkins questioned the Government’s plan for a multibillion-dollar LNG import facility as international LNG prices rose amid conflict in the Middle East. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon defended the proposal as a backup for dry-year electricity supply, arguing that it would reduce risk premiums and lower household power bills; he cited a fall in forward electricity prices after the announcement. Hipkins challenged whether the Government had assessed price and supply disruption risks and pointed to the National Infrastructure Plan’s caution that it was unclear whether LNG would lower average electricity prices. In the general debate, Green MP Scott Willis argued that reliance on internationally traded gas could expose households to price shocks, while Energy Minister Simon Watts said the country needed firming supply and blamed the previous Government’s oil and gas exploration ban for worsening energy insecurity. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said it was too early to know how the Middle East conflict would affect New Zealand, but identified potential impacts through oil prices, freight, shipping and the exchange rate.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Did the Government assess the risk of a major supply or price disruption before committing New Zealand households to pay for an LNG import facility?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I reject the characterisation of that question, because this is about lowering power bills by about $50 for every single household in this country. This is a backup source of energy, so that we don’t end up in the situation that the member and his Government created last time.

topicSummaries.topic: Food Prices and Child Poverty Put Cost-of-Living Promises Under Pressure
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Food prices and financial hardship affect household budgets directly, while child poverty figures indicate the scale of need facing families.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Barbara Edmonds challenged Finance Minister Nicola Willis to identify when grocery prices would fall, citing increases over two years of 78 percent for butter, 32 percent for mince and 22 percent for milk. Willis said the Government’s measures should make prices lower than they otherwise would have been and pointed to its policies on farm costs, employment, spending, monetary policy and tax relief, as well as efforts to increase grocery competition. Te Pāti Māori’s Mariameno Kapa-Kingi asked what immediate action the Government would take for the 170,000 children said to be experiencing poverty and hardship, including about 9,500 in Te Tai Tokerau. Child Poverty Reduction Minister Louise Upston cited tax credits, Working for Families changes and FamilyBoost, and said economic growth and jobs were central to the Government’s approach.

keyExchanges.speaker: Barbara Edmonds (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How much has the average weekly grocery bill fallen since her statement on 26 August 2025 that the Government’s next steps would “reduce food prices for Kiwis”?

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: It is clear from my statement and the work that the Government is doing that our plan is about ensuring that prices in the future would be lower than would otherwise be the case.

topicSummaries.topic: Infrastructure Plan Calls for Priorities as Parties Debate $275B Project Pipeline
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Decisions on which infrastructure to build and maintain shape public services, transport access and how taxpayers and users pay for projects.
topicSummaries.content: The House debated the National Infrastructure Plan, which identifies 11,925 projects worth $275 billion in planning or delivery and calls for better prioritisation, asset maintenance and value for money. Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop said the Government must avoid overpromising, improve planning and consider user charges, with a formal Government response due by mid-June. MPs across parties voiced support for a more stable, long-term pipeline, but disputed individual transport priorities and funding. Labour’s Kieran McAnulty said the Government had made $56 billion in transport commitments with a $30 billion funding gap. Green MP Julie Anne Genter questioned the cost-effectiveness of major road projects and argued for investment in hospitals, public transport and renewals. National and New Zealand First MPs emphasised regional roads and resilience. The House agreed to take note of the plan.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: don’t overpromise; don’t overbuild; look after what you’ve got; work out the benefit-cost ratios of things and what’s actually value for money

keyExchanges.speaker: Kieran McAnulty (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: there has been $56 billion of transport commitments made by this Government and there is a $30 billion hole in how to pay for it.

topicSummaries.topic: Police Move-On Orders Draw Criticism Over Effects on Rough Sleepers
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed powers could require people to leave public areas, including people who are begging or seeking to sleep there.
topicSummaries.content: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the Government would amend the Summary Offences Act to let police issue move-on orders for specified periods and areas. He said the powers would cover disorderly, threatening or intimidating behaviour, obstructing access to businesses, breaching the peace, begging and intending to inhabit a public place. Goldsmith cited a survey in which 91 percent of Auckland CBD operators said rough sleeping and begging negatively affected them. Green MP Tamatha Paul argued that the policy could worsen homelessness and lead to fines or imprisonment for people who cannot pay, and criticised the inclusion of people as young as 14. The transcript records the announcement and debate; it does not record passage of the proposed legislation.

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We’ve got many tools which we use to help people who are in need, but we need some extra tools to reclaim our streets for the enjoyment of those who live and work there.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tamatha Paul (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: We need cross-party consensus that homelessness is not OK and that the most cost-effective, humane way to deal with it is to house people, not to put people into prison.

topicSummaries.topic: Public Finance Bill Removes Statutory Wellbeing Reporting Requirement
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to Budget reporting rules affect what information Parliament and the public are required to receive about government decisions and their wider effects.
topicSummaries.content: In committee debate on the Public Finance Amendment Bill, Finance Minister Nicola Willis defended provisions repealing statutory requirements for wellbeing objectives and a Wellbeing Report, arguing that existing fiscal measures and Budget statements were sufficient. Labour MPs said removing the requirements could reduce transparency and weaken consistent reporting on social outcomes, including child poverty. Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan proposed adding social, infrastructure and climate-related measures to fiscal reporting; those amendments, as well as Labour’s attempt to retain the wellbeing clauses and add taxpayer estimates to a tax expenditure statement, were rejected. Part 1 of the bill, including the Government’s amendment paper, passed 68 votes to 54. The bill itself was not completed; further committee consideration was scheduled for the next sitting day.

keyExchanges.speaker: Megan Woods (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Treasury noted that the Wellbeing Report “provides a standalone piece of analysis on broader economic and social outcomes, published at regular intervals.”

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: It is simply a fiction to say that, by placing a requirement on wellbeing in the terms of the Public Finance Act, it is, in practice, changing anything about the way in which Budgets have been put together or formed.

topicSummaries.topic: Health Officials to Review Cybersecurity After Private Provider Incidents
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: A review of digital health systems and stronger safeguards could affect the protection of patients’ sensitive medical information.
topicSummaries.content: Health Minister Simeon Brown said he had asked the Ministry of Health to review the security and resilience of digital systems used across primary care after recent incidents involving private digital health providers. He said providers had been reminded of their privacy and cybersecurity obligations, and cited $19 million in additional funding for Health New Zealand’s cybersecurity capability across Budgets 2024 and 2025. The Minister of Justice had also sought advice on possible changes to Privacy Act penalties. Labour’s Ayesha Verrall pressed the Government on its oversight of private contractors holding medical records. Separately, Brown said AI scribe technology had been rolled out to all emergency departments, making it available to 1,250 staff, and that the pilot had enabled doctors to see an average of one additional patient per shift.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: government oversight … is a basic expectation when the state allows private contractors to hold intimate medical histories of its citizens.

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Is the system perfect? No. Is there more work to do? Yes.

topicSummaries.topic: KiwiSaver First-Home Rules to Be Eased for Rural Workers
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The planned changes could let some workers in employer-provided housing and aspiring farm owners use KiwiSaver savings toward a first home.
topicSummaries.content: Finance Minister Nicola Willis said the Government planned technical changes to the KiwiSaver Act so service-tenancy workers could use savings to buy a first home even if they live in employer-provided accommodation. The proposal would also allow qualifying first-time farm buyers to use KiwiSaver when purchasing through a trust, partnership or company, provided they live on the farm and meet ownership and control conditions. Willis said legislation was expected to be introduced in the middle of the year. National MP Suze Redmayne said the rules had locked some rural workers out of the first-home withdrawal scheme.

conclusion: The sitting advanced contested welfare and fiscal legislation while leaving unresolved the central political question of how to balance fiscal rules and energy security against the immediate costs and risks borne by households.
